title: Domain Name System Structure and Delegation
summary: Provides information on how names in the Domain Name System are structured, especially the top-level domains, and on how administration of domains is delegated. It is informational and does not define a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet names work like addresses: country, then city, then street. This explains who is in charge of each level of the name.

questions: how is the dns name space structured
what are the rules for delegating a domain
what is a designated manager in dns
subtitle: Who runs which part of the DNS name tree, what the original top-level domains were for, and the rules for handing a domain to a manager.

tldr.problem: As the Domain Name System grew, people needed to know how top-level names were structured and on what terms parts of the name space are handed to others to run.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the generic and country-code top-level domains, names the registries that run them, and sets out six principles for choosing and changing a designated manager of a domain.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational, not a standard. It treats a domain manager as a trustee serving the community, not an owner, and it applies the same rules recursively to every subdomain.

facts.label: Generic TLDs
facts.value: EDU, COM, NET, ORG, GOV, MIL, INT

today: RFC 1591 is an Informational memo from March 1994 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the policy as of that date, including its statement that no other TLDs than the ones listed were expected.

sections.title: Who Is in Charge
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) is the overall authority for IP addresses, domain names and many other Internet parameters. Day-to-day work is handled by the Internet Registry (IR) and regional registries, which assign IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers and most top and second level domain names.

Section 3 adds that the central IR is INTERNIC.NET, that RIPE NCC is the regional registry for Europe and APNIC for the Asia-Pacific region, and that the InterNIC administers North America and all regions not yet delegated.
sections.plainLanguage: One group keeps the master list of Internet names and numbers, and helper offices handle the daily paperwork in different parts of the world.

sections.title: The Top-Level Domains
sections.content:
The root of the DNS is unnamed. Below it are the top-level domains (TLDs): the generic ones (EDU, COM, NET, ORG, GOV, MIL and INT) and the two-letter country codes from ISO 3166. The memo says it is extremely unlikely that any other TLDs will be created.

Five generic domains are international: COM (commercial), EDU (originally all education, later limited to 4 year colleges and universities), NET (network providers' own computers), ORG (a miscellaneous bucket) and INT (organizations established by international treaties). GOV and MIL are limited to the United States. Under generic TLDs the structure is generally very flat. Country domains vary widely, and each is organized by an administrator for that country, who may delegate portions of the tree further.

The US domain is an example: names follow entity-name.locality.state-code.US, as in IBM.Armonk.NY.US, with branches in each state for schools (K12), community colleges (CC), libraries (LIB) and others. Details are in RFC 1480.
sections.plainLanguage: The top of every Internet name is like a big category label, such as company, school or country. Below each label, the people in charge decide how to organize things.

sections.title: Choosing a Designated Manager
sections.content:
A new TLD is usually created and its management handed to a designated manager all at once. The memo gives six principles, and says they apply recursively to every delegation of the name space.

  • Each domain needs a designated manager, on the Internet, with an administrative and a technical contact. For country codes at least the administrative contact must be in that country.
  • Managers are trustees who serve the community. Concerns about "rights" and "ownership" are inappropriate; "responsibilities" and "service" are the right concerns.
  • Managers must be equitable: same rules for all requests, no bias toward customers of a related business, and no required mail system or product.
  • Significantly interested parties should agree on the manager. IANA generally acts only if all contending parties agree, and an IANA-established Internet DNS Names Review Board (IDNB) rules, bindingly, when they cannot.
  • The manager must run the service competently, with a primary and a secondary nameserver. If problems persist, the delegation may be revoked.
  • For a transfer, the higher-level manager must hear from both the old and the new organization that the transfer is mutually agreed.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever runs a part of the name tree is a caretaker, not an owner. They must treat everyone fairly, run the servers well, and only hand over the job when everyone involved agrees.

sections.title: Rights to Names
sections.content:
If two registrants dispute a name, the registration authority has no role beyond giving both parties each other's contact information. Registering a domain name confers no trademark status, and the requestor must make sure they are not violating anyone's trademark.

On country codes, the IANA is not in the business of deciding what is a country. It chose the ISO 3166 list because ISO has a procedure for deciding which entities belong on it.
sections.plainLanguage: Getting a name does not make it legally yours. Disputes are for the two sides to sort out, and the name office does not decide what counts as a country.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content: The memo states that it provides information for the Internet community and does not specify an Internet standard of any kind. Its security section says only that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo explains how things are run. It does not set a standard and does not talk about security.
